title: Uber y la fintech R2 fortalecen alianza en Perú para ofrecer financiamiento
content:
Uber Technologies Inc. y R2, fintech especializada en soluciones de financiamiento digital, fortalecen su alianza en Perú para ampliar el acceso al crédito entre los socios conductores de la plataforma. Como parte del acuerdo, los conductores podrán recibir ofertas de financiamiento directamente a través de la aplicación Uber para Conductor, sin necesidad de realizar trámites presenciales.
Perú se ha convertido en el mercado de mayor aceleración del programa de financiamiento de Uber y R2 en la región, según R2. La compañía señala que este comportamiento responde a una demanda de capital entre miles de conductores que generan ingresos diariamente mediante la aplicación y que enfrentan barreras para acceder al crédito tradicional.
En el mercado peruano, el monto promedio de los préstamos otorgados bajo este programa se ubica alrededor de los US$200, mientras que el plazo promedio de pago es de aproximadamente cinco meses. El financiamiento está orientado a atender necesidades inmediatas de los socios conductores, como cubrir imprevistos o invertir en herramientas vinculadas con su actividad.
Uber y R2: financiamiento a socios conductores
El acceso al crédito se gestiona directamente desde la aplicación de Uber para Conductor. Las ofertas son preaprobadas a partir del historial de actividad del socio dentro de la plataforma, por lo que no es necesario presentar documentación adicional ni realizar trámites presenciales para acceder al financiamiento.
El esquema de pago también está vinculado a la actividad que realizan los conductores en Uber. El préstamo se cancela automáticamente mediante un porcentaje de las ganancias obtenidas por los viajes, permitiendo que los pagos se ajusten al flujo de ingresos generado por cada usuario.
La operación representa la primera colaboración conjunta de Uber y R2 en Perú. La alianza entre ambas compañías comenzó a inicios de 2025 en otros mercados de la región, inicialmente con soluciones de financiamiento dirigidas a restaurantes que operan mediante Uber Eats. Ahora, el acuerdo incorpora a los socios conductores dentro de este modelo.
Para Uber, la iniciativa busca ampliar las oportunidades económicas de sus socios conductores mediante financiamiento integrado en la plataforma que utilizan para generar ingresos. El avance del programa en Perú coincide con la expansión de R2 en América Latina, tras la inversión estratégica de Ant International para acelerar el acceso al crédito de pequeñas y medianas empresas mediante tecnología, análisis de riesgo y modelos de financiamiento embebido.
Planes de crecimiento de Uber en Perú
En entrevista con Gestión, Ángela Mendoza, gerente general de Uber para Perú, Colombia y Ecuador, señaló que 2026 será un año de consolidación para Uber en Perú, tras la expansión hacia nuevas ciudades. La estrategia tendrá tres ejes: impulsar la adopción de la aplicación, fortalecer su vínculo con el turismo y promover la educación sobre el uso de plataformas digitales de movilidad.
La compañía revisará su portafolio según las necesidades de cada mercado. Uber opera actualmente en cerca de 30 ciudades y evalúa incorporar servicios como Uber Comfort, Uber Black y mototaxi, además de UberX. Ica, Huancayo, Tacna, Cusco, Arequipa y Cajamarca figuran entre las ciudades con mayor potencial, donde la plataforma registró crecimientos de tres dígitos durante su expansión y ahora apunta a mantener tasas de doble dígito.
Uber también busca crecer mediante alianzas vinculadas al turismo, aerolíneas y eventos, además de impulsar Uber para negocios, segmento que avanza a doble dígito. Lima concentra cerca del 50% de la facturación de la compañía en el país, mientras que Perú, junto con Colombia, se encuentra entre los 15 mercados más importantes de Uber en Latinoamérica.

title: ‘Something we dreamed of’: Bangladesh celebrates historic cricket win
content:
Former players and fans hailed Bangladesh’s first-ever Test win in Australia on Sunday as the country’s biggest achievement in the five-day game, saying it could be a turning point for their cricketing ambitions.
Bangladesh sealed a historic nine-wicket thrashing inside four days in Darwin, marking their first ever Test victory on Australian soil and only second against their formidable opponents.
“This is, I think, the biggest achievement for Bangladesh cricket in Test matches,” former captain Akram Khan told AFP.
“It was something we dreamed of but perhaps none of us expected Bangladesh to dominate and win like this.
“We are extremely happy and proud.”
Akram said the big win was built on a complete team performance rather than individual brilliance.
Fast bowler Hasan Mahmud laid the foundation with a career-best 6-55 as Australia were bowled out for 198 on the opening day.
Bangladesh then took charge through Tanzid Hasan’s maiden Test century, backed by important contributions from captain Najmul Hossain Shanto and all-rounder Mehidy Hasan Miraz.
Bangladesh Cricket Board president Tamim Iqbal said the way the team outplayed Australia was “extraordinary”.
“Playing in Australia is difficult for any team,” he told reporters in Dhaka. “After 23 years, the way Bangladesh went there and played cricket and won, the credit goes 1,000 percent to them.”
Former spinner and national selector Abdur Razzak said the victory strengthened Bangladesh’s case for more Test opportunities against Australia.
This was just the seventh Test match between the teams.
“If you look at this Test and our position in the World Test Championship, there is no reason why we should not get more opportunities,” he said.
Razzak credited years of investment in domestic first-class cricket and Bangladesh’s Test programme for the team’s progress.
Former Bangladesh women’s captain Rumana Ahmed said the team’s emphatic all-round display made the win especially significant.
“Hasan Mahmud was back in the team after a long time and he did very well, taking six wickets in the first innings. That was a major factor,” she said.
“Tanzid’s hundred was historic for him as well. The batters took responsibility and scoring more than 400 in the first innings was extraordinary.”
The result was all the more remarkable because Bangladesh had been bowled out for just 54 by a Cricket Australia XI in a warm-up match days earlier.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman congratulated the team on a video call with the players.
“We’re all eagerly waiting to welcome you home,” he said on social media.
Die-hard fans also savoured the win.
“As a cricket fan of Bangladesh we don’t get occasions to celebrate very often,” Sefat Hasan Sumaiya said.
“Winning against Australia in Australia seems surreal. It feels like a national festival.”
Another fan, Sahadat Ahmed Bhuiya, called it one of the defining victories in the nation’s cricket history.
“Winning a Test in Australia within four days is a huge achievement,” he said.

title: Crawford Art Gallery update: 'We anticipate a late-2028 re-opening'
content:
Crawford Art Gallery update: 'We anticipate a late-2028 re-opening'
Construction is transforming Cork city. Apartment buildings are rising, public realm projects are progressing and at Crawford Art Gallery, the largest cultural construction project currently on site in Cork is well underway.
Transforming Crawford Art Gallery is the largest single development to date on our historic site. Alongside essential work to protect these much-loved buildings for generations, the redevelopment will enhance everything people love about Crawford while creating a gallery of international standard in the heart of Cork city.
We moved fully out of the building on January 12, 2026, which was a huge milestone for everyone involved. While it was an emotional time for the team, after months of carefully moving the collection from the gallery, we were thrilled for the moment we could hand over the site to PJ Hegarty & Sons, and the OPW.
The good news is we are eight months in to construction, and work is progressing smoothly. Much preparation was done by all parties but nothing prepares one for opening up a historic building and the surprises it will bring.
Fortunately, to date the reveals have been welcome: from old library tickets and summons letters found under floors, to parking tickets, many cigarette packs, match boxes, and additional historic fireplaces found hidden under panelling. These are all being carefully protected and documented.
Among the most fascinating discoveries are the markings left by generations of craftsmen on the building's timber structures. These are also being carefully documented as the work progresses – evidence of careful hands contributing to the building’s story over time. In fact, ‘documenting’ is a large portion of our task at the moment. There are archaeologists on site at all times, ensuring that work is carried out respectfully and that anything that is uncovered is recorded.
Work is well underway on the building's front façade. Windows, brickwork, slates, and railings are all being restored, the clock is undergoing conservation, and the new build will shortly start to emerge and be visible over the next few months.
The extension is going to be very significant for Crawford, bringing new public spaces, purpose-built collection storage, a new Learn & Explore Centre, additional galleries, a new café, improved accessibility and remarkable new views across the city. We can’t wait to experience those elevated views and celebrate Cork from a height.
The question we get asked most often is, "When are you reopening?" Progress has been smooth so far and if that continues, we anticipate handover of the building back to us in mid-2028. We will need a number of months to reinstall the artworks and get all services operating. We will provide a further update on that in mid 2027 but we anticipate a late-2028 opening.
While the building is closed, our team is planning events and continuing our programmes. Learn & Explore have continued many of their offsite community programmes, including Crawford Supported Studios and their work with Cork Migrant Centre, at alternative venues and online. They recently held some excellent events for Cork Midsummer Festival, Cork Harbour Festival, Cruinniú na nÓg, and National Heritage Week. ‘Beyond the Frame’, an outreach programme for participants in the Cork Prison, is currently holding an exhibition called Altered Images, open to the public on Spike Island.
Our conservator has been working in a temporary conservation lab set up off-site. During the decant, Dr Chiara Chillè triaged our artworks, classifying them based on the urgency of their conservation needs, and is now carrying out that work. Crawford was also recently awarded for a Heritage Stewardship Grant from the Heritage Council, which will fund much-needed, specialised conservation equipment to enable scientific analysis and support preventative conservation into the future.
Our team has been doing a phenomenal amount of research into the provenance of works and digitising archives, while also coordinating our Touring and Sharing programme.
To date we have partnered on three major exhibitions held at Uillinn: West Cork Arts Centre, the F.E. McWilliam Gallery in Banbridge, and the Highlanes Gallery in Drogheda. For anyone who is looking to visit with our collection, we still have works on loan to the Irish Museum of Modern Art, National Museum of Ireland, Michael Collins House, Doneraile Court and many more.
Our focus is now firmly on returning to the building. Over the coming months we will continue planning every aspect of reopening, from the reinstallation of the collection to visitor services, a complete rebrand, digital platforms and future staffing. We have also acquired several important new works through generous donations and look forward to sharing them with visitors when the gallery reopens.
We are thankful for the support shown to us by the Government of Ireland, the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport, the OPW, and for the excellent work by Grafton Architects Integrated Design Team and PJ Hegarty & Sons. We are also grateful for the support we have received from people who miss the gallery, as well as those who are anticipating our reopening!
We will continue to update you all throughout the redevelopment. In the meantime, we hope you enjoy this glimpse behind the scrim and feel reassured that everyone involved is working carefully, collaboratively and with great ambition to deliver the national cultural institution that Crawford — and Cork — deserve.

title: La Ville de Paris annonce la « mise à l’abri » de 250 personnes, migrantes pour la plupart, qui étaient installées sur le parvis de la mairie de Paris Centre
content:
La Ville de Paris a annoncé, samedi 22 août, « la mise à l’abri de l’ensemble des 253 personnes », des migrants essentiellement, « installées devant la mairie de Paris Centre », à la suite de l’« évacuation forcée » par l’Etat du campement établi en juillet dans l’enceinte du Samusocial, à l’occasion d’une grève d’agents de l’organisme.
Le campement, situé à proximité du quartier touristique du Marais, abritait quelque 400 personnes, dont des étrangers en situation régulière et des sans-papiers, pour certains évacués il y a plus d’une semaine du camp de fortune du Samusocial, dans le 13e arrondissement. Une situation dénoncée par les associations, qui fustigent régulièrement le manque d’hébergement d’urgence dans la capitale.
« La Ville de Paris annonce aujourd’hui l’engagement de la mise à l’abri de l’ensemble des personnes présentes sur ce site », affirme samedi la Mairie dans un communiqué. « L’ensemble des personnes installées sur le parvis de la mairie de Paris Centre sont désormais mises à l’abri au sein de gymnases de la Ville », ajoute la Mairie, « jusqu’à ce que les services de l’Etat, dont c’est la responsabilité légale et morale, leur proposent une solution pérenne ».
« C’est un véritable soulagement pour ces familles dont l’état de santé ne cessait de se dégrader », a déclaré à l’Agence France-Presse Méryl Sotty, porte-parole de Médecins sans frontières, dont les équipes ont effectué sept interventions depuis la mi-juillet sur le campement du Samusocial puis devant la mairie de Paris.
Selon Luc Viger, coordinateur pour l’Ile-de-France de l’association Utopia56, « 50 personnes restent sans solution » et vont se « retrouver dès ce soir à la permanence quotidienne de l’association », qui sollicite son réseau pour trouver des places d’hébergement chez des bénévoles.
« Je ne peux pas accepter que Paris se substitue indéfiniment à l’Etat »
Mi-août, le campement du Samusocial, qui avait rassemblé jusqu’à 450 sans-abri, a été évacué par les forces de l’ordre. « Toutes les personnes présentes sur le site du Samusocial ce matin ont reçu une proposition d’hébergement », avait alors assuré la Préfecture de police (PP) de Paris, mais « certains occupants n’ont pas souhaité bénéficier des solutions proposées et se retrouvent désormais à la rue, en pleine canicule ».
La PP et la préfecture de région avaient justifié leur décision en raison de la proximité du campement avec la route et d’un trafic « particulièrement dense ». Les autorités mettaient aussi en avant des « conditions d’hygiène » devenues « particulièrement préoccupantes » avec un « accès totalement insuffisant à l’eau et aux toilettes ».
« Je refuse que des familles et des enfants soient remis à la rue sans solution et j’ai donc pris mes responsabilités en mobilisant les moyens de la Ville pour mettre à l’abri ce matin 253 personnes », déclare le maire de la capitale, Emmanuel Grégoire, cité dans le communiqué. « Je ne peux pas accepter que Paris se substitue indéfiniment à l’Etat, alors même que l’hébergement d’urgence relève de sa responsabilité et que 300 places ont été récemment supprimées », prévient en outre l’élu socialiste.

title: Padomi supera las 360 mil atenciones de enfermería a domicilio en Lima y Callao
content:
El Servicio de Enfermería del Programa de Atención Domiciliaria (Padomi) de EsSalud realizó 360 633 atenciones domiciliarias en lo que va del año en Lima y Callao. Este trabajo permite que miles de asegurados con dificultades de movilidad reciban atención y seguimiento sin la necesidad de trasladarse a un establecimiento de salud.


Las atenciones comprenden servicios de Urgencias, Hospital en Casa, Cuidados Paliativos, Telemonitoreo, Oxigenoterapia, curaciones y otros procedimientos; además de la atención dirigida a niños a través de Padomi Niños. Para ello, se cuenta con más de 200 profesionales de enfermería, quienes se desplazan a los domicilios de los pacientes.
De estos servicios realizados, más de 166 400 corresponden a curaciones, procedimientos y seguimiento de tratamientos médicos, principalmente en adultos mayores. Estas intervenciones permiten acompañar la evolución de los pacientes y contribuir a que mantengan una mejor calidad de vida en sus propios hogares.
Acompañamiento a familias
La gerente de Oferta Flexible de EsSalud, Dra. María Emilia Isabel Hernández Vizarreta, resaltó el componente humano de esta labor y el acompañamiento que el personal brinda también a las familias. “Estas profesionales realizan una labor dedicada; no solo brindan atención, sino que también capacitan a los familiares”, señaló tras destacar su reconocimiento a estas mujeres y hombres profesionales de la salud que celebran el domingo 30 de agosto el Día de la Enfermera y del Enfermero Peruano.
Precisamente, una de las labores que complementa la atención en los domicilios es la orientación a los cuidadores. A través de la Escuela de Cuidadores Padomi, el personal de salud enseña a los familiares técnicas para realizar cambios posturales, cuidar la piel y reconocer signos de alarma que puedan requerir atención médica. Este acompañamiento busca que los familiares cuenten con herramientas para continuar con los cuidados en casa y responder a determinadas situaciones que durante la recuperación o el tratamiento de los adultos mayores.
I Congreso de Atención de Enfermería
Como parte de las acciones para fortalecer la atención de enfermería, la Subgerencia de Atención Domiciliaria Padomi organizó el I Congreso de Atención de Enfermería en el Cuidado Integral del Adulto Mayor que se desarrolla los días 27 y 28 de agosto en la sede central de EsSalud.
El encuentro tiene como objetivo reforzar los conocimientos y compartir experiencias entre los profesionales del programa. Con estas acciones, EsSalud busca fortalecer la atención domiciliaria y garantizar la continuidad de los cuidados, especialmente para los adultos mayores que requieren acompañamiento permanente; llevando atención, orientación y seguimiento hasta sus propios hogares.

title: Tajik wrestlers won five medals at the world championship in kurash in Baku
content:
Tajikistan’s national team competed at the World Championship in Kazakh kuresi (Kuresh) wrestling. The tournament took place August 21-24, 2026 in Baku (Azerbaijan).
The World Kuresi Championship was held under the auspices of United World Wrestling (UWW) – the international organization that governs Olympic wrestling styles and a number of recognized wrestling disciplines.
Participants competed for 16 sets of medals in men’s and women’s weight categories. Men competed in weight categories of 55, 60, 66, 74, 82, 90, 100, and over 100 kg. Women had categories of 48, 52, 56, 60, 65, 70, 77, and over 77 kg.
Tajikistan was represented at the world championship by a team of seven athletes. These are Muboriz Barotzoda (55 kg), Mustafoi Abdulfayz (66 kg), Huseinzoda Muhammadrajab (74 kg), Navruz Karimzod (82 kg), Haknazar Nazarov (90 kg), Emom Kamolov (100 kg), and Dadakhon Kurbonalyev (+100 kg).
Mustafoi Abdulfayz in the 66 kg weight category reached the top of the podium. Navruz Karimzod (82 kg) also won the gold medal.
Muboriz Barotzoda also performed successfully. In the 55 kg weight category, he managed to reach the final match and finished the tournament as a silver medalist.
Haknazar Nazarov (90 kg) also took second place. Muhammadrajab Huseinzoda brought another silver medal to the country. He also made it to the final and took second place.
Kazakh kuresi is a traditional Kazakh wrestling style that has significantly expanded its international reach over the past decades. Today, competitions in this sport are held far beyond Kazakhstan, and world and continental championships bring together representatives from many countries.
For Tajik spectators, this sport is particularly interesting because of its proximity to national wrestling traditions. The basis of the match is standing wrestling, grips, throwing technique, the ability to throw an opponent off balance, and the ability to execute a scoring move.
Therefore, athletes who have a solid foundation in traditional wrestling and other wrestling disciplines are able to adapt fairly quickly to the requirements of Kazakh kuresi.
The international status of Kazakh kuresi has grown noticeably in recent years. World and Asian championships are held, World Cups, European and African championships, and the geography of participants continues to expand.

title: Für 5,6 Millionen Euro - Klagenfurter Strandbad wird ab Oktober umgebaut
content:
Die Stadtwerke sanieren das Strandbad Klagenfurt ab Oktober umfassend und investieren dafür 5,6 Mio. Euro. Hauptaugenmerk ist dabei der Neubau des Mitteltrakts. Zudem übernehmen sie ab 2027 wieder den Betrieb des Strandbads Maiernigg.
Ein paar Wochen dauert es noch bis zum Ende der diesjährigen Badesaison – dann starten die umfassenden Sanierungsarbeiten im Strandbad Klagenfurt. Diese betreffen besonders den Neubau des Mitteltrakts, welcher derzeit Raum für Kiosk, Selbstbedienungs-Gastronomie und Sanitäranlagen bietet. Außerdem wird das Gebäude im Rahmen der Sanierung hochwassersicher gemacht.
Investition in moderne Technik und Infrastruktur
„Die Sanierung des Mitteltrakts ist ein weiterer Schritt in der Erneuerung des Erscheinungsbilds. Zuvor wurden bereits der Kabinentrakt im Süden des Strandbads sowie das neue Gastronomie- und Rezeptionsgebäude des Campingplatzes umgebaut“, heißt es seitens der Stadtwerke. Dafür investierten sie bereits drei Millionen Euro – für die kommenden Sanierungsarbeiten werden zusätzliche 5,6 Millionen Euro fällig.
Jene Arbeiten sind laut Stadtwerke notwendig, um Einheimischen und Gästen weiterhin ein angenehmes Freizeit- und Badeerlebnis zu bieten. Außerdem wird der Sanitärtrakt des Strandbads im Zuge des Neubaus winterfest gemacht. Damit soll die Grundlage für den ganzjährigen Betrieb möglich gemacht werden.
Auch hinsichtlich des Gastronomiebetreibers wird es einen Wechsel geben: Der aktuelle Pachtvertrag läuft noch bis zum Saisonende, danach folgt eine Neuausschreibung.
Stadtwerke übernehmen Strandbad Maiernigg
Eine Änderung gibt es auch beim Strandbad Maiernigg: Der Vertrag mit dem Pächter wird zu Jahresende aufgelöst. Danach wird das Strandbad wieder vom Eigentümer – Stadtwerke Klagenfurt – selbst geführt.
Dadurch soll der Standort langfristig abgesichert werden und zukünftig in allen drei Bädern der Stadtwerke ein einheitlich hohes Qualitäts- und Serviceangebot geboten werden. Außerdem werde ab 2027 ein neues gastronomisches Angebot geschaffen.

title: Karen Attiah Is Ready to Go Back to the Washington Post
content:
Sign up for the daily CJR newsletter.
Last fall, Karen Attiah was fired from her job as a columnist at the Washington Post over social media posts about Charlie Kirk, the conservative activist, who had just been killed. “I knew immediately that I was going to fight back,” she told me, “because it was so absurd.” Attiah, a member of the Washington-Baltimore News Guild, embarked on an arbitration process with the Post—which has now ended in her favor. In firing Attiah, the arbitrator ruled, the Post had violated its agreement with the union. “It doesn’t bring back the last year of my life,” Attiah said. “But it’s just proof that with solidarity, with unions, with a bit of grit and a bit of patience, that these fights are worth having.”
Prior to her dismissal, Attiah had worked at the Post for eleven years. Hired in 2014 as a digital producer in the Opinions section, she was the founding editor of Global Opinions before becoming a columnist. She is willing to go back, she told me, though much remains up in the air, including the nature of her role and whether she will be able to continue her Substack, where she has written regularly since her dismissal. She has not heard from the Post, she said; a spokesperson told me that the Post plans to “respect the arbitration process.” If she does return to the office, things could get awkward. But as Attiah put it: “If there’s anybody that should feel awkward, it’s going to be the people involved in making this decision. I’m very much looking forward to what walking in through those doors is going to feel like.” And if things turn sour, she told me, she may become a martial-arts influencer or a “warrior priestess of some kind for the digital age.” Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
RS: It’s been almost a year since you were fired from the Post. What did you feel at the time, and what made you want to fight the decision?
KA: I was actually home, in Dallas, because my father was quite sick. I was in town for his birthday, so it was already a stressful time. I was doing drills in kickboxing when I saw a missed call from a DC number. Not too long after that, I saw a notice-of-termination email on my phone over my Bluesky post from the previous day, in the aftermath of Charlie Kirk’s murder. I was a little bewildered. What I had said about America, about political violence, was not anywhere close, in my opinion, to controversial. They were just accurate statements about how America discusses political violence. So when I saw that the Washington Post didn’t even make a good-faith effort to have a conversation, I was in shock and bewilderment.
I knew immediately that I was going to fight back, because it was so absurd. I knew it was going to be tough. I knew it was going to be a process. But I also knew I was a part of a union, and the union kicked in pretty quickly. But in the moment, I was like, “Wow! All right, I guess I gotta glove up.”
Can you walk me though the arbitration process and what the last year has been like?
A few days after the firing, the guild asked if I wanted to file a grievance. Even at the very beginning, they said that they thought this would be a strong case. The last year has involved filing that grievance, an initial meeting with the Post in which they rejected the grievance, and then moving to arbitration. This seems like a long time. But I was also aware that going to court could possibly be even longer. We all saw this as a way to, first of all, exercise my remedies as a longtime Post guild member. And we saw this as the quickest way—as crazy as that sounds, almost a year later—to get to what we thought would be the appropriate outcome: reinstatement and vindication that my job should never have been taken in that way.
We went to the hearing, on June 4, where we presented this as if it was a court case without being in an actual court—questions, cross-examinations. The Post actually declined to cross-examine me.
Have you heard from Adam O’Neal, the Post’s former Opinions editor? What do you make of his recent departure from the Post?
I have not heard from him since we had our July 25, 2025, meeting, in which the whole Opinions section was being offered buyouts, and in which he told me that my social media was not collegial, and that my work was not consistent with his vision—a vision that he refused to articulate. He refused to tell me anything specific about what he found so objectionable. July 25 and arbitration on June 4 of this year were the only two times that I’ve been in the same room with Adam. We’ve spoken directly once so he could tell me I would no longer be continuing as a columnist.
You’ve said that the Washington Post cited security concerns arising from your posts while firing you. But they weren’t talking about security concerns for you—they were talking about other writers. Is that right?
Right. First of all, to this point of security: I’ve been on social media for thirteen to fourteen years. I was the editor who hired Jamal Khashoggi, who wrote for the Global Opinions section for a year until he was murdered, in 2018. I’ve worked with journalists who have died for expressing themselves and expressing themselves in places like the Washington Post, or with writers who’ve been jailed after writing for the Washington Post Opinions section.
The Washington Post covered itself in glory as a newspaper, as a model for how journalism outlets should behave and protect their journalists even after death. The Washington Post’s leaders at the time of the Charlie Kirk situation were being absolute cowards. At the very worst they were feeding their own journalist—me—to the wolves.
I know the Post legally has to reinstate you. Do you plan to go back?
I’ve indicated I’m willing to go back to the work that I was doing. The question for the Post is: Are they going to follow the arbitration decision? They’ve said that they respect the process, but that’s a very different question than: Are they going to comply with the outcome?
What’s happening with leadership or what’s going to happen with the Opinions section, I don’t know. What I do know is that there were people who were guild members who were fighting, who were protesting for me the whole time I was gone. And so when I think about return, I’m also thinking, Okay, I’m returning to a lot of people who fought for me.
Following the mass layoffs, I spoke with Black reporters at the Post who felt there had been a lack of commitment in the newsroom to Black journalists and to diverse coverage. Your firing was one of the things that was brought up as a concern. How are you approaching this?
This is a really heavy time for Black journalists, industry-wide. Even at the Opinions section, the fact that for a good amount of time I was the only Black woman staff writer—I always used to say that was never something I was proud of. I can probably count on one hand how many Black women staff opinion columnists there are at mainstream publications. So it is sobering to see that things have, frankly, gone quite downhill.
It’s precisely for that reason that I wanted to not go away quietly, and precisely for that reason that—as publicly humiliating as this has been—that this gave me more ability to fight back through the union process. It made me more determined to keep going, because I know that this is bigger than just me.
How much do you think the Post has changed since you worked there?
It’s very different. I came in during a time in 2014 when, gosh, it was exciting. We were doing work that was beating the New York Times in terms of traffic and subscriptions. I was helping to build this exciting new venture, Global Opinions, where we were featuring voices and journalists from all over the world. I won’t say it was perfect. We were still fighting for diverse viewpoints. We were still having to contend with challenges from people who would rather have journalists silenced. But at least it felt like we were challenging power. What has changed is, it seems, Jeff Bezos’s commitment to journalistic freedom and to wide ranges of opinions.
Seeing my colleagues who I’ve respected for a long time resigning in protest—I can’t say that that’s easy. But I think what matters is that readers out there, people care. People care so much even about what’s happening to me because they see the Washington Post to an extent as a proxy, maybe, for where America is going.
Will you still carry on with your Substack if you go back? Do you envision a post–Washington Post phase of your career?
I built an audience of fifty-six thousand subscribers, and they’ve carried me through all of this. I can’t imagine having to give up. I don’t know what the Post policies would be on that. It’s not something I’m going to give up easily. Being on Substack, being able to have a direct relationship with audiences, has been really rewarding.
When I think of my post-Post career, anyone who follows me knows that I’m an avid martial artist, and there’s a part of me that still has dreams of becoming an amateur fighter. So, if anything, my post-Post career would be being a warrior philosopher or warrior priestess of some kind for the digital age. I have a sword collection in my apartment, and I’ve been studying various forms of martial arts in my time off. I’m sure with these special skills and knowledge and weaponry that I’ve acquired in my time in exile from the Post, I can put that to an interesting use. So maybe a martial-arts influencer voice, something like that.

title: Uzbekistan marks its 35th Independence anniversary with 163 new projects
content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. As part of the celebrations marking the 35th anniversary of independence, Uzbekistan has commissioned 72 major industrial and service facilities, as well as 91 social infrastructure projects across the country.
This was reflected in the statement by the press service of the Uzbek president.
According to the statement, Mirziyoyev took part in a ceremony marking the commissioning of new facilities and stated that over the past decade, Uzbekistan has laid the foundation for what he called a new era of national development.
Furthermore, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev emphasized that investment, industrial diversification, and job creation are key factors in the country’s economic transformation.
“The last 10 years will forever be written into the history of our country as a period of laying the foundation for a new era of revival — the Third Renaissance,” Mirziyoyev said.
According to the president, Uzbekistan’s economy has grown more than 2.5 times over the past decade, while the country has attracted $160 billion in foreign investment and commissioned 2,163 major industrial facilities worth a combined $76 billion. Nearly 6 million permanent jobs have been created during the period.
Mirziyoyev stated that the country was moving away from an economy dependent on raw-material exports toward one focused on deeper processing and higher-value products.
“We are moving from a country oriented toward exporting raw materials to an economy capable of bringing finished products to global markets through deep-processing value chains,” he said.
The projects commissioned Tuesday have a combined value of nearly 50 trillion soums (about $4.2 billion) and are expected to create 15,000 jobs and generate an additional 1 trillion soums (around $84.9 million) in annual budget revenues.
The new facilities span energy, agriculture, food processing, metallurgy, automotive manufacturing, electrical equipment, construction materials, mining and textiles.
Energy projects include 1,573 megawatts of new generating capacity in Syrdarya region, a 200-MW wind farm and 100-MW energy storage system in Karakalpakstan, and renewable facilities in Navoi region expected to generate 657 million kilowatt-hours annually.
The ceremony also highlighted major investments in education and healthcare. Among the 91 social facilities are 36 kindergartens, 43 schools, seven higher education institutions and three hospitals.
The new University of New Uzbekistan complex in Tashkent covers 10 hectares and can accommodate 7,000 students. A National Library with 30,000 square meters of space was also commissioned.
Mirziyoyev stressed that the value of the projects should not be measured solely by investment and export figures.
“Every investment you make strengthens the foundation of Uzbekistan’s future. Every job you create contributes to the well-being of families,” he said.
The president officially commissioned the projects by pressing a symbolic button at the end of the ceremony.

title: Jesse Eisenberg gave a kidney to someone he’ll never meet. He still can’t get over how easy it was.
content:
About ten years ago, actor Jesse Eisenberg decided he wanted to give a kidney to a stranger. He contacted an organization to ask how, and nobody ever wrote back. That was the end of it until recently, when he mentioned the idea to a friend who works in medicine. She pointed him in the direction of NYU Langone Health in Manhattan.
He was in the hospital the next day going through the workup.
On October 30, 2025, he announced the news on the Today Show more or less by accident in the middle of a conversation about his blood donation habit. “I’m actually donating my kidney in six weeks,” he said. “I really am.”
He donated on December 30th. The technical term is “non-directed donation,” sometimes called “altruistic donation” (though transplant centers prefer the former on the grounds that all living donation is altruistic). The kidney goes to the best match on the list and the donor never finds out the recipient’s identity.
Preparing for donation
Eisenberg points out how strange it is that more people don’t do it. “When I heard about kidney donations, my first thought was, why is there not a line down the block of the hospital?” he told Dr. Mike Varshavski while on The Checkup with Doctor Mike podcast.
Months out from surgery, he told NYU Langone he’d had no lifestyle changes, no limitations, and no regrets. “I wish I had more kidneys to give,” he said.
NYU Langone puts the transplant waiting list at more than 107,000 people. Close to 95,000 of them are specifically waiting on a kidney, and roughly 13 die every day. Living donors made a bit more than 7,200 transplants possible in 2025, and their kidneys tend to last longer in the recipient than kidneys from deceased donors.
Starting a donation chain
A single, non-directed donation is usually worth more than one transplant because it can start a chain. Most people who want to give a kidney to someone specific can’t because they often aren’t a match. A stranger’s kidney breaks that logjam. Eisenberg walked Today through the hypothetical:
Someone in Kansas City needs a kidney. Their child wants to donate and isn’t a match, but Eisenberg is. His kidney goes to that person, and the child then donates to someone else who was stuck the same way. The sequence keeps unspooling as long as there are pairs waiting. None of it starts without somebody at the front of the line willing to give without getting anything back.
He also has an answer for what happens if his own mother needs a kidney next year. Through the National Kidney Foundation’s family voucher program, a donor can name specific people who then get prioritized for a living donation if they ever need one, and Eisenberg put his family on that list. He calls the whole arrangement risk-free for them as well as for himself, which is a slight oversell.
The reality is that it’s major abdominal surgery, and donors are screened hard for a reason. For most of them, however, the fifteen-year risk of kidney failure comes in under 1%, and large studies have found no increase in death or heart disease compared with people who keep both kidneys.
The momentum starts with you
His pitch is that the procedure is “essentially risk-free and so needed” and that people would come around to seeing it as obvious “if you have the time and the inclination.” Incidentally, time is what actually stops most people since donation means a few days in the hospital and several weeks of recovery, generally unpaid. That last part matters enormously to anyone without leave or savings. The other obstacle is that nothing about the system comes looking for you. Eisenberg wanted to do this for a decade, but what finally made it happen was a friend handing him a phone number.

title: Albania’s solar market shifts toward storage, market integration
content:
Albania’s solar market shifts toward storage, market integration
Albania is in the process of shifting from a solar market focused on deployment to an integrated renewable energy market, according to analysis from Dr. Lorenc Gordani, an energy market and regulatory lawyer and lecturer.
After previous estimates put Albania’s solar capacity at between 600 MW and 650 MW by the end of last year, annual data published by the country’s Energy Regulator Authority (ERE) has confirmed cumulative capacity stood at 631 MW by the end of 2025.
Gordani told pv magazine that while a consolidated official figure for new solar capacity in 2026 is not yet available, the market continues to expand strongly.
According to data released by Albania’s Institute of Statistics (INSTAT) earlier this week, electricity generated from other renewable sources during the first half of 2026 totaled 702 GWh in Albania, a 51% increase on the 464 GWh across the first half of 2025 and a 35% increase on the 519 GWh from the second half of 2025.
The figure accounts for all renewable sources other than hydropower, which is the dominant energy source in Albania and is monitored separately by INSTAT’s data collection. In the second quarter of 2026 alone, Albania generated a quarterly record of 448 GWh from other renewable sources.
Gordani added that utility-scale PV remains the main driver of investment, while commercial self-generation and distributed solar are becoming increasingly relevant.
“ERE continued to process new and modified PV licences during H1, confirming a substantial project pipeline,” he said.
Albania has introduced a new electricity sector law, No. 59/2026. The new law, which entered into force in July, introduces energy storage operations and aggregation as two additional licensed activities and permits so-called ‘active clients’ that can generate, consume, store and sell electricity. Gordani said such developments provide the basis for the next stage of electricity market development.
“The implementation process has already started at ERE level. I see this as particularly important for investors because Albania is moving towards a more structured, market-based framework, with stronger integration of renewable generation, market participation and system flexibility,” he said.
Albania is also developing a framework for self-producers of renewable energy, with rules from May establishing procedures for grid connection and compensation of renewable self-producers under a net-billing methodology. “[This] should support further growth of distributed and C&I solar,” Gordani said.
Gordani told pv magazine the biggest challenge facing Albania’s solar market is efficient integration into the electricity system, with grid capacity, balancing, flexibility and bankability becoming more important as penetration increases.
He continued that this provides a major opportunity for solar-plus-storage systems. The country’s renewable energy legislation provides a framework for support and integration of storage, Gordani said, with ERE now working to register storage operators.
Gordani also predicted continued strong growth through the remainder of 2026 in Albania’s solar market, particularly in utility-scale and C&I projects.
“However, the market is entering a more sophisticated phase where value will increasingly come from combining PV, storage, flexible generation, market participation and grid services, rather than simply adding generation capacity,” he added. “The combination of a growing PV pipeline, the new electricity-sector law, improved rules for self-producers and the emerging regulatory framework for storage creates a particularly interesting window for investors and developers in 2026–27.”
Last month, the Albanian government adopted amendments to its law governing agricultural land to allow agrivoltaics to be developed on specific categories of land.

title: 'Are you not entertained?' Sprint sensation Amy Hunt on winning four gold medals in seven days
content:
'Are you not entertained?' - Hunt enters stardom with iconic quadruple
- Published
Amy Hunt did not realise what she had done the first time she created headline-making history.
But Great Britain's new sprint sensation forewarned everyone exactly what was coming here.
Seven years ago, attending a meet in Germany primarily as part of a national junior relay squad, Hunt also decided to contest the 200m.
While Hunt, then 17, knew it was quick, she was soon informed that she had broken the under-18 women's world record.
In a time of 22.42 seconds, she had run faster than all of her childhood idols at that age.
It also bettered the British under-20 record, three months before its former holder Dina Asher-Smith won the world title.
The following year, Hunt was named as one of the 'faces to define the decade' by Vogue magazine.
Thrust into the spotlight, she was invited to an event alongside film and music stars. Hunt had travelled from her hometown of Newark, while actors such as Jacob Elordi arrived from Rome fashion week.
The world appeared to be at Hunt's feet.
Today, she knows as much as anyone that progress - especially in sport - is rarely linear.
The 24-year-old has overcome her share of setbacks to achieve a historic haul of four European gold medals in a sensational seven days on home soil.
She made no secret of her intention to become "iconic" with that unprecedented achievement, completed in Sunday's mixed 4x100m relay.
Back to full health, and her confidence in her ability fully restored, Hunt is now realising her full potential - and beginning to transcend the sport in the process.
"Are you not entertained?!" Hunt roared at the TV camera after completing her individual sprint double in Birmingham.
She had settled in immediately at Alexander Stadium with 100m gold on the opening night. Round by round and medal by medal, it became her stage - and this her championships.
She is now among the frontrunners to be named BBC Sports Personality of the Year.
But there were periods since 2019 when Hunt doubted if such moments would be possible. It would be six years until she beat her 17-year-old self over 200m.
Hunt has never been afraid to choose the hard path. Undertaking an English Literature degree at Cambridge University, she was determined to prove - as she did in winning silver at last year's World Championships - that you can be "an academic badass and a track goddess".
Once the disruption caused by the pandemic subsided, she was ready to kick on in 2022 and lined up ready to test herself against Jamaican great Elaine Thompson-Herah at an indoor meeting in Birmingham.
Fate had other ideas. Hunt left that day unable to walk, and a scan would show she had fully ruptured a tendon in her quadriceps.
To ensure a full recovery was possible, surgery followed. Requiring assistance from her mum just to get in and out of the shower, she would watch that year's Commonwealth Games in Birmingham on crutches.
Faced with the decision of whether to continue her studies, or postpone her exams and restart the year completely following her rehabilitation, Hunt powered on to avoid her final year clashing with the Olympics.
Her reward for doing so was an Olympic 4x100m relay silver medal, before a breakthrough 2025 culminated in her first individual global medal in Tokyo.
That sustained progress over recent seasons has come since she made another significant decision, uprooting her life to the north Italian city of Padua to be coached by Marco Airale.
At almost 6ft tall, which makes it difficult to accelerate out of the blocks quickly, Hunt's major area for improvement remains her start.
That will remain their focus as attention turns to rivalling the sport's greatest stars on its biggest stages.
While her least favourite of the sprint disciplines, that continues to involve winters focused on shaving time off her 60m best, which she again lowered this season to 7.04 - the eighth-fastest worldwide this year.
Hunt's major strength, meanwhile, is undoubtedly her top-end speed. In the 200m in particular, she takes great confidence in knowing few can match her in the closing stages.
"To win a global 100m nowadays, you have to run around the 10.75-second mark. Amy knows that's what she has to work towards and improving her start will get her towards that," double world 110m hurdles champion Colin Jackson told BBC Sport.
"If she wants to win the 200m, she has to be around the 21.7, 21.8-second mark, and I think she's really capable of doing that.
"I think she would look at her performances and think that she can do that. She's not far away."
While Hunt finally broke the 11-second barrier in the 100m for the first time this season, there have been unforeseen challenges as far as the 200m is concerned.
For still unknown reasons, Hunt, who lowered her 200m personal best to 22.08 in winning world silver, has struggled with low blood pressure during longer efforts which left her on the verge of fainting, including at the London Diamond League in July when finishing fifth.
Electrolytes and cold towels have been among the solutions which have helped ease those concerns as the season has progressed, and she demonstrated excellent strength to hold off Asher-Smith and Ireland's Rhasidat Adeleke in winning the European title.
Hunt is not afraid to voice her bold ambitions.
Announcing that she "wants it all" before these championships, Hunt, even in these early stages of her senior career, has demonstrated a propensity to thrive on major stages, and under ever-increasing expectation.
"Four golds was the dream and perhaps dreams do come true," said Hunt.
"It's so beyond the bounds of my dreams that I'm just euphoric. I can't believe it's happening.
"I think it will sink in later, maybe on the podium. I'm just so proud of myself and the way I've handled this week."
The Briton has already spoken about the big goal: repeating her sweep of the sprint golds at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.
Her playlist - she creates one for every major event - is already being built as she begins to visualise how that might feel.
She will be well aware how much work there is to do. So far this year, she ranks 14th-fastest worldwide in the 200m, and 25th in the 100m. Asher-Smith's British records, at 21.88 and 10.83 seconds respectively, remain untouched since 2019.
The next opportunity for global honours, beyond the inaugural World Ultimate Championships in September, will arrive at next year's World Championships in Beijing.
And, once the dust has settled on a momentous week, Hunt will set about translating continental domination to glory on the sport's biggest stages - just as British team-mate Asher-Smith achieved following her European treble in 2018.
"Amy has already won world silver, but she was not a favourite then," Jackson said.
"Now, it's a big change. She is a champion and she has to go and take on the best in the world.
"Is it going to be easy? No. But this will fill Amy with confidence. She will be on start lines trusting her ability is great, and I'm hoping that she will go from strength and strength."

title: Hong Kong lowers heat stress warning system thresholds after calls for revamp
content:
Hong Kong lowers heat stress warning system thresholds after calls for revamp
Labour Department says updates include automatically raising alert level when temperatures in multiple parts of the city reach 35 degrees Celsius
Hong Kong labour authorities have unveiled changes to the system that sends out warnings to workers about overexertion during very hot weather, reducing thresholds so higher-tier alerts can be issued more easily following intense criticism of the mechanism.
The Labour Department said on Thursday that two new conditions would be introduced to the Heat Stress at Work Warning system from Friday.
The system has three warning levels – amber, red and black – which alert employers and staff to the severity of heat stress if they are working outdoors or indoors without air conditioning.
The first change will reduce the threshold for triggering a higher-tier warning if the Observatory has already issued the extremely hot weather special alert, to ensure a quicker response.
The second change will see the warning automatically be raised by one level – from amber to red, or from red to black – when the measured temperatures generally over Hong Kong reach 35 degrees Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) or above.
The revamp was introduced after the system faced criticism over the lack of higher alerts earlier this month, when the city was grappling with record-breaking temperatures.

title: Korea donates 1,000 Kiswahili-translated Folktale Books to Tanzanian children
content:
Korea donates 1,000 Kiswahili-translated Folktale Books to Tanzanian children
DAR ES SALAAM: TANZANIAN children are set to journey into the rich world of Korean culture and traditional storytelling after the Republic of Korea donated 1,000 copies of Korean folktale books translated into Kiswahili to the Tanzania Institute of Education (TIE).
The donation is aimed at strengthening reading skills while giving young Tanzanians an opportunity to discover Korean stories in a language they understand best.
The handover ceremony, held in Dar es Salaam, marked another step in the growing educational and cultural partnership between Tanzania and Korea.
The books are expected to provide children with enjoyable reading materials while exposing them to Korean traditions, values and cultural heritage through engaging stories.
Speaking during the ceremony, Ambassador of the Republic of Korea to Tanzania, Eunju Ahn, said the books would serve as a bridge between the two nations by bringing Korean stories closer to Tanzanian children. She emphasized that sharing stories across languages and cultures can help young people develop curiosity, appreciation and a deeper understanding of other societies.

TIE Director General, Dr Aneth Komba, expressed appreciation for Korea’s continued support and assured that the donated books would be fairly distributed among schools and effectively utilized for the benefit of students. She also expressed interest in strengthening cooperation between TIE and Korea, particularly in initiatives aimed at improving educational opportunities for Tanzanian children.
The donation comes as part of a broader partnership between Korea and Tanzania in the education sector. Since 2021, Korea has worked with TIE through the Korea-Led ICT Cooperation (KLIC) Programme, supporting digital education through ICT equipment, capacity-building programmes for teachers and education officers, and knowledge-sharing on the development of digital learning content.
Ambassador Ahn reaffirmed Korea’s commitment to supporting Tanzania’s development, particularly through education, describing young people as one of the country’s most valuable assets for the future. With the donation, a simple book becomes more than a reading resource—it becomes a cultural bridge, connecting Tanzanian children with Korea through the universal power of stories.

title: Dopo un ictus i cani diventano alleati preziosi per i pazienti in riabilitazione
content:
Dopo un ictus i cani diventano alleati preziosi per i pazienti in riabilitazione
Indice
Spazzolare il pelo di un cane con la mano da riabilitare. Camminargli accanto lungo un corridoio. Lanciargli una pallina e recuperare, nel frattempo, un po’ di movimento. Alla Mayo Clinic alcune normali sedute di riabilitazione dopo un ictus sono state costruite intorno a queste attività. E i pazienti coinvolti si sono mossi di più, sono rimasti attivi più a lungo e hanno partecipato con maggiore coinvolgimento alla terapia rispetto a chi seguiva soltanto il programma standard. Lo mostra un trial randomizzato pubblicato su Mayo Clinic Proceedings.
Il risultato merita però una misura precisa. Lo studio riguarda 50 persone ricoverate dopo un ictus, seguite in un singolo programma ospedaliero, e mostra soprattutto un effetto sulla partecipazione e sull’attività durante le sedute. Non autorizza ancora a dire che un cane faccia recuperare più velocemente capacità motorie o autonomia nel lungo periodo. Su questo serviranno studi più grandi e un follow-up più lungo.
Il cane entra negli esercizi, non fa semplicemente compagnia
I ricercatori hanno assegnato casualmente i 50 pazienti a due gruppi. Il primo ha seguito la normale riabilitazione ospedaliera, che comprendeva fisioterapia, terapia occupazionale e logopedia. Nel secondo gruppo, composto da 25 persone, alcune sedute sono state svolte insieme a cani da terapia e ai loro conduttori. I partecipanti potevano effettuare da una a sei sessioni, della durata di 30 minuti ciascuna e distribuite nell’arco massimo di due settimane.
Un dettaglio cambia parecchio la lettura dello studio: le sessioni con i cani sostituivano alcune normali sedute riabilitative, non venivano semplicemente aggiunte aumentando le ore di terapia. La differenza osservata, quindi, non può essere liquidata con un banale “hanno fatto più esercizio perché sono rimasti più tempo in palestra”.
Il cane diventava parte dell’esercizio. Si poteva camminare al suo fianco, giocare al riporto, accarezzarlo o spazzolarlo, adattando l’attività agli obiettivi riabilitativi del singolo paziente. Un movimento ripetitivo resta un movimento ripetitivo; se alla sua estremità c’è un cane che aspetta la pallina, evidentemente può cambiare parecchio la voglia di farlo. La Mayo Clinic descrive proprio motivazione ridotta, poca energia, solitudine e scarso interesse per gli esercizi tra gli ostacoli che possono pesare sulla riabilitazione dopo un ictus.
Più partecipazione e più attività durante le sedute
La differenza più netta riguarda il coinvolgimento. I pazienti del gruppo con i cani hanno ottenuto punteggi significativamente più alti nella Pittsburgh Rehabilitation Participation Scale, utilizzata dai terapisti per valutare quanto una persona partecipa attivamente al trattamento. La differenza statistica tra i gruppi aveva un valore di p=0,0038.
Anche i sensori utilizzati per misurare il movimento hanno registrato più attività fisica per minuto nel gruppo con terapia assistita dal cane, con p=0,023, e una percentuale maggiore del tempo trascorsa in movimento, con p=0,006. È questo il dato concreto dietro l’idea dei pazienti che “camminano di più”: durante quelle sedute erano effettivamente più attivi e rimanevano mobili più a lungo.
Sono emerse anche differenze in due parametri della variabilità della frequenza cardiaca, utilizzata come indicatore della regolazione del sistema nervoso autonomo. Secondo gli autori, i cambiamenti osservati sono compatibili con una migliore risposta allo stress durante le sessioni. L’umore e gli altri parametri fisiologici misurati, compresa l’ossitocina salivare, non hanno invece mostrato differenze statisticamente significative tra i due gruppi. Il cane, insomma, non ha fatto miracoli ormonali: ha soprattutto reso i pazienti più partecipi e fisicamente attivi.
Lo studio è piccolo e non basta per parlare di recupero più rapido
Il campione resta ridotto. Nel solo gruppo sperimentale c’erano 25 persone, 17 uomini e 8 donne, con un’età media di circa 65 anni; 19 si sono identificate come bianche. Lo studio si è svolto alla Mayo Clinic di Rochester, in Minnesota, tra febbraio 2023 e febbraio 2024. Sono caratteristiche che restringono parecchio la possibilità di estendere automaticamente i risultati a tutti i pazienti colpiti da ictus.
Soprattutto, tra gli indicatori considerati dagli autori c’erano anche qualità della vita, umore e recupero funzionale, mentre gli effetti statisticamente più chiari pubblicati riguardano motivazione, partecipazione e quantità di movimento durante la riabilitazione. È una distinzione importante: essere più coinvolti nel trattamento è certamente interessante, ma rimane da verificare se sedute più frequenti o programmi più lunghi riescano a trasformare questo vantaggio in un recupero clinico maggiore nelle settimane e nei mesi successivi.
C’è inoltre un elemento da mettere sul tavolo insieme ai risultati: la ricerca è stata finanziata da Nestlé Purina PetCare Global Resources e condotta in collaborazione con l’azienda. Il finanziamento non invalida i dati, naturalmente, però appartiene alle informazioni necessarie per leggerli nella loro interezza e viene dichiarato dagli stessi autori.
E i cani come vivono queste sedute?
C’è anche l’altra metà della terapia, quella con quattro zampe. Lo stesso gruppo di ricerca aveva già pubblicato nel 2025 uno studio prospettico randomizzato sul benessere dei 14 cani da terapia con i rispettivi conduttori coinvolti nel programma di riabilitazione per l’ictus. Venivano controllati frequenza cardiaca, variabilità cardiaca, temperatura timpanica, cortisolo e ossitocina nella saliva, oltre ai comportamenti collegati allo stress.
Dopo le sessioni i cani mostravano una frequenza cardiaca più bassa e una maggiore variabilità cardiaca; cortisolo, ossitocina e comportamenti associati allo stress non presentavano variazioni significative. Gli autori hanno quindi concluso che, nelle condizioni studiate e con animali selezionati e conduttori qualificati, le attività non sembravano produrre uno stress misurabile nei cani. Alcuni parametri suggerivano persino uno stato di maggiore rilassamento.
È anche questo a distinguere un intervento strutturato dalla semplice idea di portare un cane in reparto sperando che faccia bene a tutti. Qui gli animali erano addestrati, lavoravano insieme ai loro conduttori e le attività venivano integrate negli obiettivi terapeutici.
Per ora il risultato più solido rimane molto concreto: durante alcune sedute di riabilitazione dopo un ictus, 50 pazienti sono bastati per osservare che la presenza di un cane può rendere il lavoro più coinvolgente e, soprattutto, far muovere di più chi deve ricominciare a farlo. Per sapere se quelle mezz’ore lasciano anche un segno più profondo sul recupero servirà il passo successivo della ricerca. Il cane, intanto, la pallina è già pronto a riportarla.
Fonte: Mayo Clinic Proceedings

title: Už sází stromy. Proměna plzeňského náměstí, která rozhádala památkáře, jde do finále
content:
Článek
Těch stromů zde bude stát do pátku celkem čtrnáct, v přibližně desetimetrových rozestupech vytvoří alej od morového sloupu ke kašně zvané Chrtice. Jsou zhruba deset let staré a do Česka přicestovaly už počátkem jara z Nizozemska.
„Jde o druh odolávající současným klimatickým výkyvům,“ uvedl arborista David Hora. „Roste rychle, a to až do patnáctimetrové výšky, v dobrých podmínkách může dosáhnout stáří osmdesáti let, koruna je široká deset metrů. Pro Plzeň jsme vybrali kultivar odolný proti grafióze, nemoci postihující jilmy,“ vysvětlil Hora.
Nová pěší zóna
Zmíněná strana náměstí, kde stojí třeba biskupství nebo hotel Central, se proměnila v pěší zónu výškově splývající s dlažbou ve středu náměstí. Vozovka zmizela, naznačuje ji pouze skladba dlažby. Auta se sem už nedostanou, tedy s výjimkou zásobování.
Přibyl mobiliář, třeba stojany na kolo nebo kousek od pasáže Slavie moderně pojaté osvěžující mlžítko. Akce, která už pět měsíců komplikuje život hlavně chodcům a místním obchodníkům, ale ještě nekončí. Zbývá řada dodělávek, třeba doposud nejsou osazené nové lampy. „Hotovo bude prvního září,“ řekl Novinkám primátor Roman Zarzycký (ANO).
Rozhádaní památkáři
Revitalizace náměstí vychází z návrhu, s nímž v roce 2024 vyhrálo brněnské studio MAAUS městem vypsanou architektonickou soutěž. Reálný výsledek, konkrétně ořezávání historických desek takzvané plzeňské žulové dlažby, označilo zdejší pracoviště Národního památkového ústavu (NPÚ) ve svém červnovém stanovisku za „…svévolné a neobhajitelné ničení jedné z kulturně historických a památkových hodnot městské památkové rezervace…“.
Vedoucí památkového odboru magistrátu Karel Zoch na to reagoval: „Upravená dlažba umožní rovinnější položení a bude tedy pro uživatele veřejného prostoru komfortnější. Charakter dlažeb tak zůstane zachován a přiblíží se podobě z konce devatenáctého století.“
Státním památkářům vadí i stromy bránící pohledům na katedrálu, na náměstí v novodobé historii rostly akorát v květináčích, a třeba i nahrazení historizujících lamp moderně pojatým osvětlením. Nezávisle na NPÚ šel i podnět k památkové inspekci ministerstva kultury.
„Doteď není znám výsledek,“ sdělil Petr Sokol, ředitel plzeňského NPÚ. „Neočekávám, že by na západní straně ještě došlo k nějaké změně, ale jde o případný postup při dalších fázích rekonstrukce.“
V následných etapách se mimo jiné počítá s vysazením stromů i na opačné straně náměstí. „Probíhá projektová příprava, která by měla být do roka hotova,“ uvedl primátor. „Včetně úpravy Dřevěné ulice půjde o nějakých dvě stě až dvě stě padesát milionů, bude tedy záležet na politické vůli i na možnostech rozpočtu, kdy dojde na vlastní realizaci,“ uzavřel Zarzycký.

title: First day of school comes with excitement, bittersweet feelings
content:
Sign up for Chalkbeat Detroit’s free newsletter to keep up with the city’s public school system and Michigan education policy.
Jasmine Ng had mixed feelings about starting her junior year Monday morning at Stoney Creek High School in Rochester Hills. She was excited to arrive with all her siblings — her little sister, who’s at Stoney Creek, too, and her little brother, who’s starting at Hart Middle School, right across the street.
“Usually it’s just me and my sister. Today, it was, ‘Yay let’s go to school together for the first time since COVID,’” Ng said.
But amid the first day excitement, Ng was also thinking about the SAT season looming in the distance. She said she’s not looking forward to taking those tests her junior year, when many kids start the college application process.
Miles away in Detroit, as students at East English Village Preparatory Academy at Finney returned to school Monday morning, staff made sure the teens were amped up and ready to take on the day. A DJ played Montell Jordan’s “This Is How We Do It,” as school leaders and community members clapped and cheered on students as they entered the building for the annual “clap-in.”
“Good morning!” the crowd exclaimed as a girl with long braids waved shyly as she passed by. “Happy first day!”
Monday marked the first day of school in some suburban school districts and the Detroit Public Schools Community District. Students returned with excitement and jitters as they entered freshly cleaned schools, greeted their new teachers, and reconnected with their friends. Across metro Detroit, the 2026-27 school year will have a lot in store for students, teachers, and school leaders. Three months from now, voters will elect a new governor who will have the power to push for dramatic changes to address poor test scores.
Students will have to become accustomed to new state rules that restrict the use of wireless devices such as cell phones during instruction, and gym classes that will now have to include a fitness test. On the plus side, the state once again will provide free school meals to public school students, regardless of income. And high school juniors, some of whom are preparing for college admissions essays, will have one fewer to write with the elimination of the SAT essay exam they usually would take in the spring as part of the Michigan Merit Exam.
In Detroit, city and school leaders are expanding efforts to curb chronic absenteeism. The city will continue to provide free bus service to all Detroit students through the Detroit Department of Transportation and is launching a new program offering rideshare service to students at four high schools. DPSCD is expanding its program that pays high school students for perfect attendance, adding middle school students this school year. And the district is expanding a program that provides yellow school bus service at high schools with particularly high rates of chronic absenteeism.
Here’s what the first day looked like in multiple schools:
State’s new policy forces teens to ‘disconnect from our cell phones’
At East English Village, senior Ortez Matthews said he’s ready to begin his final year. He’s taking two advanced placement classes, an honors class, and some career and technical education courses on top of extracurriculars like student council, coaching baseball and serving on Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield’s youth cabinet.
He said he doesn’t mind putting his cell phone away for most of the day to comply with the state’s new student policy restricting the use of wireless devices during instruction.
“I do think that our generation, Gen Z, do need to disconnect from our cell phones for some time because when we were growing up, we always had them. School is somewhere to start because at home, we can do whatever we want.”
The clap-in that greeted students was organized by school staff and the DPSCD Foundation. Kerrie Mitchell Campbell-Mabins, president and CEO of the foundation, said she wanted to make sure students felt loved and supported.
“This is a representation of what they can expect all year, that the community is going to be out to support them and to make sure that they have everything that they need,” Campbell-Mabins said.
Vitti emphasizes good attendance in school visits
DPSCD Superintendent Nikolai Vitti visited several schools across the district Monday. He fielded questions from students that touched on a variety of topics, including when they would get paid for perfect attendance, why they have to wear uniforms, and whether he likes Jordan basketball shoes.
Sixth graders at Carstens Elementary-Middle School on the city’s east side shared highlights of their summer breaks: a trip to Cedar Point, dinner at Red Lobster, and lots of swimming.
In a seventh grade classroom at Nolan Elementary-Middle School on the north side of Detroit, some students expressed their dislike of the new cell phone policy requiring them to put their devices away until the end of the day.
“I bet if I come back around December and I ask you to compare this year versus last year, you’ll say you’re more focused on what happens in the classroom because you don’t have your phone,” Vitti said to the kids.
At Southwest Detroit’s Bennett Elementary School, Vitti reminded a class of third graders about the importance of coming to school every day.
Principal Melissa Villarreal helped translate the message into Spanish.
“What do I tell you every Monday?” Villarreal said. “We have to be here because when we’re not, it gets really hard to reach your goals, right?”
A cold start to the first day of school
At Stoney Creek High in Rochester Hills, school buses rounded the traffic circle, dropping kids off in the 50-something degree weather that Principal Brian Shelson said was the coldest first day in the school’s history.
Many older students with driver’s licenses opted to drive to school. Addison Fogler, a senior from Rochester who spent the summer up north with her family, got together with friends last night to decorate their cars in a school-wide senior tradition.
“We wrote like Seniors 2027, lots of dots and hearts,” she said.
Monday morning she picked up some of her best friends and they listened to songs mixing nostalgia with excitement, to match the feeling of finally arriving for the final year of high school.
“‘Ribs’ by Lorde, ‘Where’d Time Go?’ All the classics,” she said.
Mobolaji Akimbiyi, a Stoney Creek junior, is planning to take the SAT in two weeks. He used the summer to study, in addition to resting, doing AP language homework, and watching the World Cup with his dad. He’s most excited for AP Physics.
Like Ng, Akimbiyi has mixed feelings about the first day — a combination of excitement, apprehension, and a bit of relief to be back in routine after a languid few months.
“Summer kind of dragged on,” he said.
A final first day at a Detroit school set to close
A slow trickle of a couple dozen students with shiny see-through plastic backpacks gathered in front of the door at Detroit’s Thurgood Marshall Elementary-Middle School on the city’s north end. They waited patiently as teachers decked out in blue greeted them.
Though the group assembled for the clap-in was small, spirits were high as upbeat music and staff cheers welcomed the children inside.
“Welcome back, welcome back,” staff cheered as they danced with excitement.
The school, which had around 170 students in 2025-26, is set to close at the end of June due to low enrollment and high costs. Its closure follows that of four other DPSCD schools last year.
Evan Pringle, who will start ninth grade at Oak Park High School Tuesday, met up with his brothers outside of Marshall around 8:30 a.m. He attended Marshall from preschool through eighth grade.
“I’m sad,” he said of the school’s impending closure. “But, I already knew it was gonna happen because they’ve been saying that since I was in like fifth grade.”
Chalkbeat Detroit Bureau Chief Lori Higgins contributed to this report.
Beki San Martin is a reporter for the Detroit Free Press. You can reach her at RSanMartin@freepress.com.
Hannah Dellinger covers Detroit schools for Chalkbeat Detroit. You can reach her at hdellinger@chalkbeat.org.
Micah Walker is a reporter for BridgeDetroit. You can reach her at mwalker@bridgedetroit.com.
